@@ -0,0 +1,410 @@
+/**
+ * Lua
+ *
+ * A grammar for Lua 5.4's syntax, following the shape of Lua's own reference-manual
+ * grammar (section 9) closely, with real `{% %}` JavaScript actions building a tagged-
+ * object AST for every rule. Authored directly in Gramaire's native `.gram` format
+ * (ADR D36, promoted to first-class alongside `.gram.md`) rather than as literate
+ * Markdown — its prose survives as plain banner and doc comments, exactly the shape a
+ * Sphinx site's MyST-Parser extension would consume verbatim, with no Markdown-to-RST
+ * translation needed.
+ *
+ * Two deliberate simplifications, both documented at the rule that needs them:
+ *
+ *   - Statement separators (`;`) are MANDATORY here, unlike real Lua's optional ones.
+ *     Lua's own manual documents a genuine ambiguity when they're optional (a statement
+ *     ending in a call-like expression, immediately followed by a new statement starting
+ *     with `(`, can read as one statement or two); real implementations resolve it with a
+ *     lexer-level heuristic outside the grammar. Gramaire's LR(1) table builder has no
+ *     such escape hatch — an undeclared conflict is a hard build error, not a silent
+ *     shift-preference default — so this grammar closes the ambiguity by requiring the
+ *     separator instead of leaving it optional.
+ *   - Long bracket strings/comments (`[[...]]`, `--[[...]]`) are supported at level 0
+ *     only; `[=[...]=]` and deeper (an arbitrary, unbounded, matching `=` count) are not
+ *     regular languages and cannot be expressed as a fixed regex — the same class of gap
+ *     `examples/antlr/antlr4.gram.md` documents for ANTLR's brace-balanced `ACTION`
+ *     token. See the Tokens section below.
+ *
+ * The expression grammar needs no `## Precedence`-equivalent declarations at all: Lua's
+ * `-` (unary minus vs. binary subtract) and `~` (unary bnot vs. binary bxor) each share
+ * one token across two precedence tiers — exactly the case yacc's `%prec` directive
+ * exists for, and Gramaire has no equivalent (a production's precedence is always its
+ * last terminal's declared level). Instead, every one of Lua's eleven precedence tiers
+ * is its own nonterminal in a strict chain (the classic precedence-climbing technique),
+ * so the automaton never has to choose between "reduce the unary production" and "shift
+ * a lower-tier binary operator" — the grammar is unambiguous by construction.
+ */
+
+%name Lua
+%lang javascript
+
+/// An identifier. Keyword-vs-identifier overlap needs no special handling — a quoted
+/// literal keyword (`'and'`, `'function'`, ...) beats an overlapping identifier class
+/// automatically, via the same maximal-munch precedence every other Gramaire grammar
+/// relies on.
+NAME : /[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*/
+
+/// A numeral: decimal (optionally fractional, optionally exponented) or hexadecimal
+/// (optionally fractional, with a `p`/`P` exponent instead of `e`/`E`). All non-capturing
+/// — the action reads the token's own full matched text, the convention every Gramaire
+/// example uses (see e.g. examples/json.gram.md's NUMBER).
+NUMBER : /0[xX](?:[0-9a-fA-F]+(?:\.[0-9a-fA-F]*)?|\.[0-9a-fA-F]+)(?:[pP][-+]?[0-9]+)?|(?:[0-9]+(?:\.[0-9]*)?|\.[0-9]+)(?:[eE][-+]?[0-9]+)?/
+
+/// A short string, single- or double-quoted, with backslash escapes. Gramaire's regex
+/// dialect forbids backreferences, so "the same quote that opened it" can't be expressed
+/// directly — writing the two quote styles as separate alternatives sidesteps that
+/// entirely. Escape sequences are recognized structurally (`\\.` — anything after a
+/// backslash) but not decoded: an action reading a STRING's value gets the quotes
+/// stripped and the escapes left as literal source text, not interpreted. Decoding all of
+/// Lua's escape forms (`\n`, `\ddd`, `\xXX`, `\u{XXX}`, `\z`, ...) is a runtime concern
+/// orthogonal to the grammar's actual purpose (syntax, not evaluation), so it's left to
+/// whatever consumes the AST.
+STRING : /"(?:[^"\\\n]|\\.)*"|'(?:[^'\\\n]|\\.)*'/
+
+/// A long-bracket string, level 0 only (`[[...]]`) — see the file banner's note on why
+/// `=`-leveled long brackets (`[=[...]=]` and deeper) are out of scope.
+LONGSTRING : /\[\[(?:[^\]]|\][^\]])*\]\]/
+
+/// A long-bracket comment, level 0 only (`--[[...]]`) — same limitation as LONGSTRING.
+/// Declared before the line-comment token below; maximal munch prefers whichever
+/// actually matches longer at a given position, so a `--[[` that has no matching `]]`
+/// anywhere in the file simply falls through to a same-line line comment instead — never
+/// a lexical error, just a shorter match.
+LONGCOMMENT : /--\[\[(?:[^\]]|\][^\]])*\]\]/   %skip
+
+/// A line comment, running to end of line.
+COMMENT : /--[^\n]*/   %skip
+
+/// Whitespace, including newlines — Lua has no layout-sensitive syntax.
+WS : /[ \t\r\n]+/   %skip
+
+/// A block is a sequence of statements, each terminated by `;` (see the file banner's
+/// note on why the separator is mandatory here), optionally ending in a `return`.
+/// A block used as a statement's BODY (a function/do/while/for/if branch) may be empty —
+/// every such use site marks it `Block?` and defaults to an empty block when absent. The
+/// top-level `Chunk` is the one exception: Gramaire's `lr` notation has no way to express
+/// a production with zero right-hand-side symbols at all (the same root cause behind
+/// `examples/antlr/antlr4.gram.md`'s documented "empty alternative" gap), so a literal
+/// empty/whitespace-only source file is the one thing this grammar cannot accept.
+Chunk
+  : Block   {% (c) => c.block %}
+
+Block
+  : stmts:Stmt+ ret:ReturnStat?   {% (c) => ({ tag: "Block", statements: c.stmts, ret: c.ret ?? null }) %}
+  | ret:ReturnStat                 {% (c) => ({ tag: "Block", statements: [], ret: c.ret }) %}
+
+/// One statement plus its mandatory terminator — never itself a semantic node in the AST.
+Stmt
+  : Statement ';'   {% (c) => c.statement %}
+
+/// A `return`, always the last thing in a block (so, unlike every other statement, its
+/// trailing `;` can stay genuinely optional — nothing ever follows a `return` for the
+/// mandatory-separator rule to disambiguate against).
+ReturnStat
+  : 'return' values:ExprList? ';'?   {% (c) => ({ tag: "Return", values: c.values ?? [] }) %}
+
+/// A statement. Matches Lua's own reference grammar's `stat` production directly, one
+/// alternative per real Lua statement form.
+Statement
+  : '::' name:NAME '::'
+      {% (c) => ({ tag: "Label", name: c.name }) %}
+  | 'break'
+      {% (c) => ({ tag: "Break" }) %}
+  | 'goto' name:NAME
+      {% (c) => ({ tag: "Goto", name: c.name }) %}
+  | 'do' body:Block? 'end'
+      {% (c) => ({ tag: "Do", body: c.body ?? { tag: "Block", statements: [], ret: null } }) %}
+  | 'while' cond:Expr 'do' body:Block? 'end'
+      {% (c) => ({ tag: "While", cond: c.cond, body: c.body ?? { tag: "Block", statements: [], ret: null } }) %}
+  | 'repeat' body:Block? 'until' cond:Expr
+      {% (c) => ({ tag: "Repeat", body: c.body ?? { tag: "Block", statements: [], ret: null }, cond: c.cond }) %}
+  | 'if' cond:Expr 'then' thenBody:Block? elseifs:ElseifClause* elsePart:ElsePart? 'end'
+      {% (c) => ({
+           tag: "If",
+           cond: c.cond,
+           thenBody: c.thenBody ?? { tag: "Block", statements: [], ret: null },
+           elseifs: c.elseifs ?? [],
+           elseBody: c.elsePart ?? null
+         }) %}
+  | 'for' name:NAME '=' start:Expr ',' stop:Expr step:ForStep? 'do' body:Block? 'end'
+      {% (c) => ({
+           tag: "ForNum",
+           name: c.name,
+           start: c.start,
+           stop: c.stop,
+           step: c.step ?? null,
+           body: c.body ?? { tag: "Block", statements: [], ret: null }
+         }) %}
+  | 'for' names:NameList 'in' exprs:ExprList 'do' body:Block? 'end'
+      {% (c) => ({
+           tag: "ForIn",
+           names: c.names,
+           exprs: c.exprs,
+           body: c.body ?? { tag: "Block", statements: [], ret: null }
+         }) %}
+  | 'function' name:FuncName body:FuncBody
+      {% (c) => ({ tag: "FunctionDecl", name: c.name, body: c.body }) %}
+  | 'local' 'function' name:NAME body:FuncBody
+      {% (c) => ({ tag: "LocalFunction", name: c.name, body: c.body }) %}
+  | LocalDecl
+      {% (c) => c.localDecl %}
+  | targets:VarList '=' values:ExprList
+      {% (c) => ({ tag: "Assign", targets: c.targets, values: c.values }) %}
+  | FunctionCall
+      {% (c) => c.functionCall %}
+
+/// One `elseif` branch of an `if` statement.
+ElseifClause
+  : 'elseif' cond:Expr 'then' body:Block?
+      {% (c) => ({ cond: c.cond, body: c.body ?? { tag: "Block", statements: [], ret: null } }) %}
+
+/// An `if` statement's trailing `else` branch. Its own explicit `'else'` keyword is what
+/// makes the position unambiguous — without one, an empty `elseif`/`then` body would be
+/// indistinguishable from "the next statement actually belongs to this branch."
+ElsePart
+  : 'else' body:Block?
+      {% (c) => c.body ?? { tag: "Block", statements: [], ret: null } %}
+
+/// The optional `, step` clause of a numeric `for`.
+ForStep
+  : ',' step:Expr   {% (c) => c.step %}
+
+/// A `local` declaration: a comma-separated list of attributed names and an optional
+/// initializer list.
+LocalDecl
+  : 'local' names:AttribNameList init:LocalInit?
+      {% (c) => ({ tag: "Local", names: c.names, init: c.init ?? [] }) %}
+
+/// The `= expr, ...` initializer of a `local` declaration.
+LocalInit
+  : '=' values:ExprList   {% (c) => c.values %}
+
+/// A comma-separated list of one or more attributed names.
+AttribNameList
+  : names:Comma<AttribName>   {% (c) => c.names %}
+
+/// A name with its optional `<const>`/`<close>` attribute (Lua 5.4).
+AttribName
+  : name:NAME attrib:Attrib?   {% (c) => ({ name: c.name, attrib: c.attrib ?? null }) %}
+
+/// A `<const>`/`<close>` variable attribute.
+Attrib
+  : '<' name:NAME '>'   {% (c) => c.name %}
+
+/// A function declaration's name: a base name, zero or more dotted path segments, and an
+/// optional trailing `:method` name.
+FuncName
+  : base:NAME path:FuncNamePath* method:FuncNameMethod?
+      {% (c) => ({ tag: "FuncName", base: c.base, path: c.path ?? [], method: c.method ?? null }) %}
+
+FuncNamePath
+  : '.' name:NAME   {% (c) => c.name %}
+
+FuncNameMethod
+  : ':' name:NAME   {% (c) => c.name %}
+
+/// A function body: a parameter list and a block, sharing `end` with its enclosing
+/// `function`/`local function` statement or `function` expression.
+FuncBody
+  : '(' params:ParList? ')' body:Block? 'end'
+      {% (c) => {
+           const ps = c.params ?? [];
+           const varargAt = ps.findIndex((p) => p.tag === "Vararg");
+           const named = varargAt === -1 ? ps : ps.slice(0, varargAt);
+           return {
+             tag: "FuncBody",
+             params: named.map((p) => p.name),
+             vararg: varargAt !== -1,
+             body: c.body ?? { tag: "Block", statements: [], ret: null }
+           };
+         } %}
+
+/// A parameter list: a comma-separated name list with an optional trailing `...`, or a
+/// bare `...` (a function taking only varargs).
+/// A parameter: a plain name, or Lua's vararg marker `...`. Real Lua additionally
+/// requires a `...` (if present) to be the LAST parameter — a semantic constraint this
+/// grammar doesn't enforce structurally. Modeling it as `namelist [',' '...']` instead
+/// (matching Lua's own reference grammar literally) would need the parser to decide,
+/// right at a comma, whether it continues the name list or introduces a trailing
+/// vararg — genuinely unresolvable with LR(1)'s one token of lookahead, since both
+/// continuations look identical until the token AFTER the comma. Folding `...` into the
+/// same comma-list as an ordinary element sidesteps the ambiguity entirely.
+Param
+  : NAME    {% (c) => ({ tag: "Name", name: c.name }) %}
+  | '...'   {% (c) => ({ tag: "Vararg" }) %}
+
+ParList
+  : params:Comma<Param>   {% (c) => c.params %}
+
+/// A comma-separated list of one or more names.
+NameList
+  : names:Comma<NAME>   {% (c) => c.names %}
+
+/// A comma-separated list of one or more assignment targets.
+VarList
+  : vars:Comma<Var>   {% (c) => c.vars %}
+
+/// A comma-separated list of one or more expressions.
+ExprList
+  : exprs:Comma<Expr>   {% (c) => c.exprs %}
+
+/// A prefix expression: a variable, a function call, or a parenthesized expression.
+/// Parenthesizing truncates a call's multiple results to exactly one value under real
+/// Lua semantics — this grammar models only the syntax, not that runtime truncation.
+PrefixExpr
+  : Var                    {% (c) => c.var %}
+  | FunctionCall           {% (c) => c.functionCall %}
+  | '(' expr:Expr ')'      {% (c) => c.expr %}
+
+/// An assignable location: a bare name, an indexed table field, or a dotted field.
+/// Mutually recursive with PrefixExpr/FunctionCall, matching Lua's own reference
+/// grammar exactly — the shared left-recursive prefix chain (`NAME`, then any run of
+/// `[expr]`/`.field`/`:method(args)`/`(args)` continuations) is what lets an LR(1)
+/// parser tell a bare variable from the start of a function call, deferring the
+/// decision until it sees which continuation (or none) actually follows.
+Var
+  : NAME                                  {% (c) => ({ tag: "Name", name: c.name }) %}
+  | base:PrefixExpr '[' index:Expr ']'    {% (c) => ({ tag: "Index", base: c.base, index: c.index }) %}
+  | base:PrefixExpr '.' field:NAME        {% (c) => ({ tag: "Field", base: c.base, field: c.field }) %}
+
+/// A function or method call.
+FunctionCall
+  : callee:PrefixExpr args:Args
+      {% (c) => ({ tag: "Call", callee: c.callee, method: null, args: c.args }) %}
+  | callee:PrefixExpr ':' method:NAME args:Args
+      {% (c) => ({ tag: "Call", callee: c.callee, method: c.method, args: c.args }) %}
+
+/// A call's arguments: a parenthesized expression list, a bare table constructor, or a
+/// bare string literal — the latter two are Lua's syntactic sugar for a single-argument
+/// call (`f{...}`, `f"..."`).
+Args
+  : '(' args:ExprList? ')'   {% (c) => c.args ?? [] %}
+  | TableConstructor          {% (c) => [c.tableConstructor] %}
+  | STRING                    {% (c) => [{ tag: "Str", value: c.string.slice(1, -1) }] %}
+
+/// A table constructor: `{}`, or a brace-delimited list of fields.
+TableConstructor
+  : '{' fields:FieldList? '}'   {% (c) => ({ tag: "Table", fields: c.fields ?? [] }) %}
+
+/// A comma- or semicolon-separated list of one or more table fields, with an optional
+/// trailing separator.
+FieldList
+  : fields:Sep<Field, FieldSep> trailing:FieldSep?   {% (c) => c.fields %}
+
+FieldSep
+  : ',' | ';'
+
+/// A table field: `[expr] = expr` (a computed key), `name = expr` (a string key), or a
+/// bare expression (a positional/array-style element). Structurally identical to Lua's
+/// own reference grammar's `field` production, including the same NAME-vs-bare-expr
+/// prefix ambiguity `Var`/`FunctionCall` already resolve the same way.
+Field
+  : '[' key:Expr ']' '=' value:Expr   {% (c) => ({ tag: "ComputedField", key: c.key, value: c.value }) %}
+  | key:NAME '=' value:Expr            {% (c) => ({ tag: "NamedField", key: c.key, value: c.value }) %}
+  | value:Expr                         {% (c) => ({ tag: "PosField", value: c.value }) %}
+
+/// The full expression grammar is a strict precedence-climbing chain, lowest tier first
+/// (see the file banner's note on why — no `%left`/`%right` declarations anywhere below).
+Expr
+  : OrExpr   {% (c) => c.orExpr %}
+
+/// Tier 1 (lowest): logical or, left-associative.
+OrExpr
+  : left:OrExpr 'or' right:AndExpr   {% (c) => ({ tag: "Or", left: c.left, right: c.right }) %}
+  | AndExpr                           {% (c) => c.andExpr %}
+
+/// Tier 2: logical and, left-associative.
+AndExpr
+  : left:AndExpr 'and' right:CmpExpr   {% (c) => ({ tag: "And", left: c.left, right: c.right }) %}
+  | CmpExpr                             {% (c) => c.cmpExpr %}
+
+/// Tier 3: relational/equality comparisons, left-associative.
+CmpExpr
+  : left:CmpExpr op:CmpOp right:BOrExpr
+      {% (c) => ({ tag: "Cmp", op: c.op, left: c.left, right: c.right }) %}
+  | BOrExpr   {% (c) => c.bOrExpr %}
+
+CmpOp
+  : '<' | '>' | '<=' | '>=' | '~=' | '=='
+
+/// Tier 4: bitwise or, left-associative.
+BOrExpr
+  : left:BOrExpr '|' right:BXorExpr   {% (c) => ({ tag: "BOr", left: c.left, right: c.right }) %}
+  | BXorExpr                            {% (c) => c.bXorExpr %}
+
+/// Tier 5: bitwise xor (binary `~`), left-associative — distinct from unary bnot, which
+/// lives at the unary tier further down and shares the same token.
+BXorExpr
+  : left:BXorExpr '~' right:BAndExpr   {% (c) => ({ tag: "BXor", left: c.left, right: c.right }) %}
+  | BAndExpr                             {% (c) => c.bAndExpr %}
+
+/// Tier 6: bitwise and, left-associative.
+BAndExpr
+  : left:BAndExpr '&' right:ShiftExpr   {% (c) => ({ tag: "BAnd", left: c.left, right: c.right }) %}
+  | ShiftExpr                             {% (c) => c.shiftExpr %}
+
+/// Tier 7: bit shifts, left-associative.
+ShiftExpr
+  : left:ShiftExpr op:ShiftOp right:ConcatExpr
+      {% (c) => ({ tag: "Shift", op: c.op, left: c.left, right: c.right }) %}
+  | ConcatExpr   {% (c) => c.concatExpr %}
+
+ShiftOp
+  : '<<' | '>>'
+
+/// Tier 8: string concatenation, right-associative (`a..b..c` is `a..(b..c)`).
+ConcatExpr
+  : left:AddExpr '..' right:ConcatExpr   {% (c) => ({ tag: "Concat", left: c.left, right: c.right }) %}
+  | AddExpr                                {% (c) => c.addExpr %}
+
+/// Tier 9: addition/subtraction, left-associative — distinct from unary minus, which
+/// shares the `-` token but lives at the unary tier further down.
+AddExpr
+  : left:AddExpr op:AddOp right:MulExpr   {% (c) => ({ tag: "Arith", op: c.op, left: c.left, right: c.right }) %}
+  | MulExpr                                 {% (c) => c.mulExpr %}
+
+AddOp
+  : '+' | '-'
+
+/// Tier 10: multiplication/division/floor-division/modulo, left-associative.
+MulExpr
+  : left:MulExpr op:MulOp right:UnaryExpr
+      {% (c) => ({ tag: "Arith", op: c.op, left: c.left, right: c.right }) %}
+  | UnaryExpr   {% (c) => c.unaryExpr %}
+
+MulOp
+  : '*' | '/' | '//' | '%'
+
+/// Tier 11: unary operators (`not`, `#`, `-`, `~`), binding tighter than every binary
+/// operator above but looser than `^` below. Recurses into itself (not a binary tier),
+/// which is exactly why the two operators it shares a token with (`-`/binary subtract,
+/// `~`/binary xor) never create a conflict: there is no item set where the automaton
+/// must choose between reducing this production and shifting a binary operator, since
+/// this nonterminal has no route back up to a binary-tier production.
+UnaryExpr
+  : op:UnaryOp operand:UnaryExpr   {% (c) => ({ tag: "Unary", op: c.op, operand: c.operand }) %}
+  | PowExpr                          {% (c) => c.powExpr %}
+
+UnaryOp
+  : 'not' | '#' | '-' | '~'
+
+/// Tier 12 (highest): exponentiation, right-associative, and binding tighter than unary
+/// on its LEFT but allowing unary on its RIGHT (`-2^2` is `-(2^2)`; `2^-2` is valid) —
+/// exactly what recursing into UnaryExpr (not PowExpr) on the right encodes.
+PowExpr

+package gramaire.lab
+
+// A conformance-style check that examples/lua.gram is "genuinely runnable," not just
+// structure-passing: parses a real, multi-construct Lua snippet (recursion, if/else,
+// a table constructor, a numeric for, a function call) through the real engine and
+// confirms both acceptance and a working self-contained evaluator, matching
+// LabApiSuite's own conventions (JVM-only: reads a real file from examples/).
+import gramaire.Method
+
+class LabApiLuaSuite extends munit.FunSuite:
+  private def readFile(path: String): String =
+    java.nio.file.Files.readString(java.nio.file.Path.of(path))
+
+  private lazy val luaGram = readFile("examples/lua.gram")
+
+  private val factorial =
+    """local function fact(n)
+      |  if n <= 1 then
+      |    return 1;
+      |  else
+      |    return n * fact(n - 1);
+      |  end;
+      |end;
+      |local t = { 1, 2, x = "hi", [10] = true };
+      |for i = 1, 3 do
+      |  print(i);
+      |end;
+      |""".stripMargin
+
+  test("evaluate: a real multi-construct Lua snippet builds and is accepted") {
+    val resp = LabApi.evaluate(LabRequest(luaGram, Some(factorial), Method.Canonical))
+    assert(resp.buildOk, s"expected buildOk, diagnostics: ${resp.diagnostics}")
+    assertEquals(resp.diagnostics.filter(_.severity == "error"), Vector.empty)
+    resp.parse match
+      case None       => fail("expected a parse result")
+      case Some(pass) => assert(pass.accepted, s"expected the snippet to be accepted: $pass")
+    assert(resp.evaluatorJs.isDefined, "a real, working evaluator should be baked")
+  }
+
+  test("evaluate: the mandatory-`;` simplification actually rejects the omitted-separator form") {
+    // Two statements juxtaposed with no `;` between them, the exact shape real Lua's own
+    // manual documents as ambiguous (assignment immediately followed by a parenthesized
+    // prefixexp) — this grammar closes the ambiguity by requiring the separator, so
+    // omitting it must be a hard rejection, not silently accepted one way or the other.
+    val noSemicolon = "local x = 1\n(print)(x);\n"
+    val resp = LabApi.evaluate(LabRequest(luaGram, Some(noSemicolon), Method.Canonical))
+    assert(resp.buildOk, s"expected buildOk, diagnostics: ${resp.diagnostics}")
+    resp.parse match
+      case None       => fail("expected a parse result (rejected, not a build failure)")
+      case Some(pass) => assert(!pass.accepted, "omitting the mandatory `;` must be rejected")
+  }
+
+  test("evaluate: the same snippet WITH the separator inserted is accepted") {
+    val withSemicolon = "local x = 1;\n(print)(x);\n"
+    val resp = LabApi.evaluate(LabRequest(luaGram, Some(withSemicolon), Method.Canonical))
+    assert(resp.buildOk, s"expected buildOk, diagnostics: ${resp.diagnostics}")
+    resp.parse match
+      case None       => fail("expected a parse result")
+      case Some(pass) => assert(pass.accepted, s"expected acceptance with the separator present: $pass")
+  }
